parts.move: state the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor and each symbol's meaning
parts.prompt: State the equation for the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire, defining each symbol and the angle.
scheme: F = BIl sinθ
B is the flux density, I the current, l the length of wire inside the field
θ is the angle between the current direction and the field
parts.answer: The force is F = BIl sinθ, where B is the magnetic flux density, I the current, l the length of wire lying in the field and θ the angle between the current and the field. Maximum force at 90°; zero when parallel.

parts.move: state the magnetic force on a moving charge and its direction rule
parts.prompt: State the equation for the magnetic force on a moving charge in a magnetic field, and state what determines its direction.
scheme: F = BQv when the velocity is perpendicular to the field (F = BQv sinθ in general)
The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field
Use the right-hand rule: for positive charge, point along v, curl toward B, thumb gives F
parts.answer: A charge Q moving at speed v at right angles to a field B feels F = BQv, directed perpendicular to both velocity and field — given by the right-hand rule for positive charge (reverse for negative). The force steers but never speeds up or slows down the charge.

parts.move: explain why a field-parallel velocity produces no magnetic force
parts.prompt: Explain why a charged particle moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force, and what happens when it moves perpendicular instead.
scheme: The force depends on sinθ: only the velocity component across the field contributes
Parallel motion gives sinθ = 0, so F = 0
Perpendicular motion maximises sinθ = 1, giving F = BQv and a circular path
parts.answer: The magnetic force is proportional to the velocity component cutting across the field, BQv sinθ. Motion along the field lines has no transverse component (sin 0° = 0) and is ignored by the field; perpendicular motion gives the full BQv, which continuously deflects the charge into a circle. At a general angle, the parallel part sails straight while the transverse part curves the path into a helix.

parts.move: explain the helical trajectory of a charge entering at an angle to the field
parts.prompt: A non-relativistic charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at an angle between parallel and perpendicular. Neglect all other forces and radiation losses. Describe its trajectory and explain why the pitch stays constant.
scheme: The perpendicular velocity component produces circular motion because B|Q|v_perp supplies the centripetal force
The parallel component is unchanged because there is no magnetic force along the field, producing a helix
The parallel speed and circular period remain constant, so the distance advanced along the field per turn (pitch) is constant
parts.answer: Resolve the velocity along and perpendicular to the field. The perpendicular component undergoes circular motion with B|Q|v_perp as the centripetal force. The parallel component has no magnetic force and stays constant, so the combined path is a helix. The period 2πm/(B|Q|) is constant in the uniform field; constant parallel speed times constant period gives constant pitch.

parts.move: apply F = BIl sinθ to find the force on a length of current-carrying wire
parts.prompt: A straight wire segment of length 0.050 m carries 3.0 A at 40° to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the magnetic force on it. (sin 40° = 0.643)
scheme: Direction from the right-hand rule, perpendicular to wire and field
parts.answer: F = BIl sinθ = 0.20×3.0×0.050×0.643 = 0.019 N, directed perpendicular to both the wire and the field — the principle that moves loudspeaker voice coils.

parts.move: apply F = BQv as a centripetal force to find an orbit radius
parts.prompt: A proton (m = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, Q = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 4.0×10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. Calculate the radius of its circular path.
scheme: Magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: BQv = mv²/r
Rearrange to r = mv/(BQ)
Radius = 8.35×10⁻² m, approximately 8.4 cm
parts.answer: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: BQv = mv²/r. Cancelling v and rearranging gives r = mv/(BQ). Substituting gives r = (1.67×10⁻²⁷×4.0×10⁶)/(0.50×1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 8.35×10⁻² m = 8.35 cm, or 8.4 cm to two significant figures.

parts.move: reject the claim that a magnetic force increases a charge's kinetic energy
parts.prompt: A student says the magnetic force accelerates a moving charge and increases its speed. Explain why its speed cannot change, and what does change.
scheme: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity
A perpendicular force does no work: it changes direction, not magnitude
The charge's speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only its path direction changes
parts.answer: Because the magnetic force always acts at right angles to the velocity, it does no work on the charge — W = Fd cos90° = 0. Its speed and kinetic energy are untouchable; only the direction of motion turns. Any actual speeding-up requires an electric field.

parts.move: reject identifying the force on a wire with a Newton's-third-law pair
parts.prompt: A wire in a field experiences F = BIl. A student labels the equal and opposite force as 'the wire pushing back on the field' and draws it on the wire's free-body diagram. Identify both errors.
scheme: The third-law pair acts on the magnet/source of the field, not on the wire — it belongs on a different body's diagram
Only forces on the wire itself belong on the wire's free-body diagram
The pair force is real but must not be double-counted as a second force on the wire
parts.answer: Both errors are free-body errors. The third-law partner of the field's force on the wire acts on the magnet or current producing the field — it is never an extra force on the wire. A free-body diagram shows only forces applied to the body in question: draw F = BIl on the wire, its reaction elsewhere.

parts.move: combine electric and magnetic force balance to find a selected velocity
parts.prompt: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of 2.0×10⁵ V m⁻¹ is crossed with a magnetic field of 0.40 T. Calculate the speed of particles that pass through undeflected, and explain the force balance.
scheme: Undeflected requires EQ = BQv: electric and magnetic forces balance
parts.answer: The selected particle feels EQ from the plates and BQv from the field in opposite directions; they cancel exactly when v = E/B = 2.0×10⁵/0.40 = 5.0×10⁵ m s⁻¹. Charges of either sign pass — the mass and charge cancel — only the speed is selected.

parts.move: combine electric acceleration with magnetic deflection to find a mass-related radius
parts.prompt: A singly ionised ion is accelerated from rest through 500 V then enters a 0.080 T field perpendicular to its velocity. Derive the path radius in terms of the ion's mass and evaluate it for mass 1.0×10⁻²⁵ kg. (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: Acceleration: eV = ½mv² → v = √(2eV/m)
In the field: r = mv/(eB)
Substituting v: r = m√(2eV/m)/(eB) = √(2mV/e)/B
parts.answer: The accelerating voltage gives v = √(2eV/m); the field turns this into r = mv/eB = √(2mV/e)/B. For a 1.0×10⁻²⁵ kg ion at 500 V in 0.080 T, r = √(2×10⁻²⁵×500/1.6×10⁻¹⁹)/0.080 ≈ 0.25 m. The radius grows as √m — heavier ions curve less, which is exactly how a mass spectrometer sorts them.

parts.move: combine circular motion with magnetic deflection to derive the cyclotron frequency
parts.prompt: Show that the time for one complete circle of a charged particle in a magnetic field is independent of its speed, and calculate the cyclotron frequency for a proton in a 1.2 T field. (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: Period T = 2πr/v with r = mv/(BQ)
T = 2πm/(BQ) — the v cancels completely
parts.answer: With r = mv/BQ, the period T = 2πr/v = 2πm/BQ — the speed cancels: faster particles travel bigger circles in exactly the same time. The cyclotron frequency is f = BQ/2πm = 1.2×1.6×10⁻¹⁹/(2π×1.67×10⁻²⁷) ≈ 18 MHz, which is why one fixed radiofrequency drives a cyclotron at all speeds.
